title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Mrs. Jennings was a widow with a generous income settled on her at marriage. She had only two daughters and had lived to see both respectably married. Nothing therefore remained for her to do except marry off the rest of the world. She worked at this with all the energy her abilities allowed, missing no opportunity to plan weddings among the young people she knew. She was remarkably quick to discover attachments, and had enjoyed making many a young lady blush and feel important by hinting at her influence over a particular young man. This gift of perception enabled her, soon after arriving at Barton, to declare with certainty that Colonel Brandon was deeply in love with Marianne Dashwood. She suspected it on their very first evening together because he listened so attentively to Marianne’s singing. When the Middletons returned the visit by dining at the cottage, his listening again settled the matter. It must be true; she was entirely convinced. They would make an excellent match: he was rich, and she was beautiful. Ever since her connection with Sir John had brought Colonel Brandon into her acquaintance, Mrs. Jennings had wanted to see him well married. And she was always eager to find a good husband for every pretty girl.

The immediate benefit to herself was substantial, since the discovery provided an endless supply of jokes at both their expense. At the park she teased the colonel; at the cottage she teased Marianne. He probably cared nothing about the jokes, so far as they concerned only himself. Marianne at first could not understand them. Once she understood their point, she scarcely knew whether to laugh at their absurdity or condemn their impertinence. She thought them an unfeeling comment on the colonel’s great age and his lonely situation as an old bachelor.

Mrs. Dashwood could not consider a man five years younger than herself quite as ancient as her daughter’s youthful imagination made him. She ventured to suggest that Mrs. Jennings probably had no intention of making fun of his age.

“But Mama, even if you do not think the accusation deliberately unkind, you must admit how absurd it is. Colonel Brandon is certainly younger than Mrs. Jennings, but he is old enough to be my father. If he ever had enough spirit to fall in love, he must have outlived such feelings long ago. It is too ridiculous! When can a man be safe from jokes like these, if age and infirmity offer him no protection?”

“Infirmity!” Elinor said. “Do you call Colonel Brandon infirm? I can quite understand that he seems much older to you than to Mama. But surely you cannot persuade yourself that he has lost the use of his limbs!”
“Did you not hear him complain of rheumatism? And is that not the most common affliction of advancing age?”
“My dearest child,” her mother said, laughing, “by that reasoning you must live in constant fear of my decline. It must seem miraculous to you that I have survived to the advanced age of forty.”

“Mama, you are being unfair to me. I know perfectly well that Colonel Brandon is not yet old enough for his friends to fear losing him through natural causes. He may live another twenty years. But thirty-five has no business with marriage.”

“Perhaps,” Elinor said, “thirty-five and seventeen ought not to have any business with marrying each other. But if there happened to be a woman still single at twenty-seven, I should not consider Colonel Brandon’s being thirty-five any reason against his marrying _her_.”

“A woman of twenty-seven,” Marianne said after a brief pause, “can never expect to feel or inspire love again. If her home is uncomfortable or she has little money, I can imagine her agreeing to act as a nurse in return for a wife’s maintenance and security. There would therefore be nothing unsuitable in his marrying such a woman. It would be an arrangement of convenience, and society would be satisfied. I should not call it a marriage at all, but that would not matter. To me it would seem simply a business exchange, each party hoping to profit at the other’s expense.”

“I know it would be impossible,” Elinor replied, “to persuade you that a woman of twenty-seven might feel anything close enough to love for a man of thirty-five to make her want him as a companion. But I must object to your sentencing Colonel Brandon and his wife to permanent confinement in a sickroom merely because yesterday, on a very cold, damp day, he happened to mention a slight rheumatic pain in one shoulder.”
“But he spoke about flannel waistcoats,” Marianne said. “And to me a flannel waistcoat always means aches, cramps, rheumatism, and every other complaint that can trouble the old and feeble.”

“If he had only been suffering from a violent fever, you would not have despised him half so much. Admit it, Marianne: do you not find something appealing in the flushed cheeks, sunken eyes, and racing pulse of a fever?”

Soon afterwards, when Elinor left the room, Marianne said, “Mama, I have a fear about illness that I cannot keep from you. I am sure Edward Ferrars is unwell. We have been here nearly a fortnight, and still he does not come. Nothing but real illness could explain such an extraordinary delay. What else could keep him at Norland?”

“Did you expect him to come so soon?” Mrs. Dashwood asked. “I did not. Indeed, if I have felt any anxiety about it, it has been because I remember how little pleasure or eagerness he sometimes showed in accepting my invitation when I spoke of his coming to Barton. Is Elinor already expecting him?”
“I have not mentioned it to her, but naturally she must be.”

“I rather think you are mistaken. Yesterday, when I spoke to her about buying a new fireplace grate for the spare bedroom, she said there was no immediate hurry, since we were unlikely to need the room for some time.”

“How strange! What can it mean! But their entire behaviour towards each other has been impossible to explain! Their last farewells were so cold, so calm! Their conversation on their final evening together was so lifeless! Edward said goodbye to Elinor exactly as he did to me, offering us both the good wishes of a loving brother. Twice on that last morning I deliberately left them alone together, and each time, for no understandable reason, he followed me out. And when Elinor left Norland and Edward, she did not cry as I did. Even now she never loses her self-control. When does she seem miserable or low-spirited? When does she try to escape company, or seem restless and unhappy in it?”
